questions.question: What is a 'regression' in software engineering?
options: A new feature that was never built
A bug where a change accidentally breaks something that previously worked correctly
questions.explanation: A regression specifically means previously working functionality broke because of a new change — automated tests exist largely to catch this class of bug immediately.

questions.question: What is 'technical debt'?
options: Money owed to a cloud provider for compute usage
The accumulated future cost of shortcuts taken to ship faster now, which make future changes slower or riskier if unaddressed
A type of bug that only appears in production
The time it takes to write documentation
questions.explanation: Technical debt is a deliberate or accidental trade-off: shipping faster now at the cost of future changes being harder, similar to how financial debt trades present benefit for future cost (interest).

questions.question: A stakeholder asks why a feature that 'works when I tried it' can't ship today without more testing and review. Which question best reframes this productively?
options: Can we just skip testing this one time?
What specific regression or edge-case failure would our current tests and review process catch that manual clicking wouldn't?
Why do engineers need to test anything ever?
Can we remove code review from the process permanently?
questions.explanation: Testing and code review exist to catch specific failure modes (regressions, edge cases, single-author blind spots) that manual, happy-path testing typically misses — grounding the conversation in concrete risk rather than abstract process.
